# Anatomy of a Multiple-Choice Item {background-color="#14497F" .center}

## The parts of an item

::: {.incremental}
* ***Stem*** — the part that contains the core question or statement.
* ***Options*** — the answer choices provided, consisting of:
  * ***Key*** — the correct answer.
  * ***Distractors*** — incorrect choices, but designed to still seem plausible.
:::

::: aside
[Lane, Raymond, & Haladyna (2016)](https://books.google.de/books?hl=id&lr=&id=GDCvCgAAQBAJ&oi=fnd&pg=PP1&dq=Lane,+Raymond,+%26+Haladyna+(2016)&ots=pM3NPfplBv&sig=8dUxIKgAlIlv8FyMJNQ6ZCgZXAQ&redir_esc=y#v=onepage&q&f=false).
:::

## Why these parts need to be clearly separated

::: {.incremental}

* The *stem* and *options* serve different functions.
  + The *stem* conveys **one** clear core idea.
  + While the *options* provide alternative answers that are equivalent in form.

* A good item doesn't mix the two, for example by putting part of the essential information in only one of the *options*.

:::

# Writing the Stem {background-color="#14497F" .center}

## Basic principles

::: {.incremental}
* State the core idea clearly and concisely in the stem, don't tuck it away in the options.
* Use positive phrasing; avoid negative forms such as "EXCEPT" or "NOT", which are easy to miss when reading and increase the risk that test-takers misunderstand the instruction.
  + So if a test-taker answers incorrectly, you'll have a hard time telling whether they genuinely couldn't answer or simply misread the instruction.
* Limit each item to a single type of content and a single level of cognitive process (Meeting 3).
* Match the complexity of the language to the group who will take the test; avoid sentences that are long and rambling.
:::

::: aside
[Haladyna, Downing, & Rodriguez (2002)](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1207/S15324818AME1503_5).
:::

# Writing the Answer Options {background-color="#14497F" .center}

## Principles for the *key* and *distractors*

::: {.incremental}
* Make sure there is only **one** correct answer, with no ambiguity.
* Make the *distractors* plausible.
  + Ideally, base them on common misconceptions about the topic, rather than choices that are obviously wrong or impossible.
* Keep the length and grammatical structure of all options consistent; an option that is noticeably longer or more detailed often gives away the correct answer.
* Avoid absolute words like "*always*" or "*never*" in a distractor, since they tend to be easy to spot as the wrong answer.
:::

## Principles for the *key* and *distractors*

::: {.incremental}
* Avoid options like "*all of the above*" or "*none of the above*".
  + These can often be answered correctly without truly understanding the other options.
* Randomize the position of the correct answer across items; don't always place it in the same spot.
* Order the options logically — alphabetically or by numerical value, for example — whenever possible.
:::

::: aside
[Haladyna, Downing, & Rodriguez (2002)](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1207/S15324818AME1503_5).
:::

# Writing Achievement Test Items vs. Aptitude Test Items {background-color="#14497F" .center}

## Different test substance

::: {.incremental}
* **Achievement test items** are derived from the TIK (learning objectives) already formulated ([Meeting 4](/slides/pertemuan4-en.qmd)).
  + Their content is tied to the material or curriculum being taught.
* **Aptitude test items** are derived from the definition of a more general ability construct ([Meeting 5](/slides/pertemuan5-en.qmd) and [6](/slides/pertemuan6-en.qmd)).
  + Their content is deliberately kept independent of any one subject area, so that what's measured is the reasoning process itself, not specific knowledge.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Practical implication
When writing an achievement test item, you start from the TIK. When writing an aptitude test item, you start from the *narrow ability* you want to measure. For example, *induction* or *quantitative reasoning* from the *broad ability* Gf discussed in [Meeting 6](/slides/pertemuan6-en.qmd).
:::

# Example Aptitude Test Items {background-color="#14497F" .center}

## Based on *narrow abilities* from Gf

Three *narrow abilities* commonly measured on aptitude tests ([Meeting 6](/slides/pertemuan6-en.qmd)):

::: {.incremental}
* ***Induction*** — discovering the rule underlying a pattern.
* ***General sequential reasoning*** — drawing a logical conclusion from given premises.
* ***Quantitative reasoning*** — reasoning using numerical relationships and operations.
:::

## Example: *induction*

*"SHOE : FOOT, as ... : ..."*

(A) Earring : Ear <br> (B) Nest : Bird <br>　(C) Vegetable : Pot <br> (D) Brush : Paint

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Key
**A** — the relationship between a body part and the item worn/used on it, just like a shoe on a foot.
:::

## Example: *general sequential reasoning*

*"All flowers have a pistil. All jasmines are flowers."*

(A) All jasmines have a pistil <br> (B) Some jasmines do not have a pistil <br> (C) Some flowers are not jasmines <br> (D) All flowers are jasmines

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Key
**A** — a direct logical conclusion drawn from the two premises (categorical syllogism).
:::

## Example: *quantitative reasoning*

*"3, 6, 12, 24, ..."*

(A) 30 <br> (B) 36 <br> (C) 48 <br> (D) 60

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Key
**C (48)** — pattern: each term is multiplied by 2.
:::

# Example Achievement Test Item {background-color="#14497F" .center}

## Derived from a TIK

Using the TIK from Meeting 4: *"Students can match each principle of achievement test construction with an example of it."*

::: {.callout-note}
#### Example item
*"The principle of 'measuring a representative sample of content' in an achievement test is best illustrated by:"*

(A) A final exam that contains questions only from the last meeting

(B) A final exam whose questions are spread evenly across all meetings

(C) A final exam with a uniform level of difficulty

(D) A final exam with a large number of questions
:::

::: aside
Answer: B.
:::

## Activity: Spotting Errors in an Item

The item below has several problems. Discuss what needs to be fixed.

::: {.callout-important}
#### What's wrong with this item?
*"Which of the following statements is NOT a characteristic of an aptitude test?"*

(A) Always measures an innate ability present from birth that can never change at all over a person's lifetime

(B) Is predictive of future performance

(C) Is not tied to any one specific subject area

(D) All of the above are correct
:::

. . .

::: {.incremental}
* The stem uses a negative word ("NOT"), which should be avoided.
* Option A uses absolute words ("always", "can never", "at all"), which gives away that this option is wrong.
* Option D ("all of the above are correct") should be avoided, per the principle discussed today.
* Some answer options are written too long.
:::

## Summary

::: {.incremental}
1. A multiple-choice item consists of a *stem*, *key*, and *distractors*, and each has its own function and writing principles.
2. The *stem* is written clearly, concisely, and positively; the core idea belongs in the *stem*, not the *options*.
3. The *options* are made equal in length and structure, with plausible *distractors*, free of absolute words or "all/none of the above" choices.
4. Achievement test items are derived from the TIK; aptitude test items are derived from the *narrow ability* being measured.
:::
